variants.name: Rails controller action wrapped in ActiveRecord::Base.transaction
variants.idiom_name: ActionController action with an ActiveRecord::Base.transaction block
variants.implementation_notes: The low-ceremony Rails realization: the controller action is the script - it reads params, does the work, and wraps the multi-step part in ActiveRecord::Base.transaction { }, which commits on normal exit and rolls back when an exception escapes the block (raise ActiveRecord::Rollback to roll back without propagating the exception). A single-record save or destroy is already wrapped in a transaction by Active Record, so a trivial action needs no block; add the block as soon as the request performs several writes that must succeed together. after_commit/after_rollback hooks are the sanctioned place for side effects triggered by the script.
variants.code_sketch:
class BookingsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    booking = ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
      room = Room.lock.find(params[:room_id])
      raise NotAvailable unless room.free?(params[:from], params[:to])
      room.bookings.create!(from: params[:from], to: params[:to])
    end
    render json: { id: booking.id }, status: :created
  end
end
pitfalls: ActiveRecord::Rollback is swallowed by the transaction block while other exceptions are re-raised - rescue the wrong one and failures pass silently.
after_commit callbacks fire only once the outermost transaction commits, so side effects enqueued inside the script run later than the script's own return.
Rescuing ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid inside the block leaves the transaction unusable on PostgreSQL; let it abort and handle it outside.

variants.name: One class per script (service object / use case) with a single public call
variants.idiom_name: Service object class (def call / def perform) wrapping its steps in a transaction
variants.implementation_notes: The Rails community's refinement of the pattern for anything beyond a trivial action: one class per use case, constructed with its inputs and exposing a single public method (call/perform) that wraps the steps in ActiveRecord::Base.transaction and returns a result object. The controller shrinks to a delegation, the script gets a name that can be referenced from routes, jobs and tests, and duplication between actions becomes visible; dry-operation formalizes the same shape with typed step results. It is still a procedure, not a domain object - the point is a named, testable script, not an object model.
variants.code_sketch:
class BookRoom
  def initialize(room_id, from, to)
    @room_id, @from, @to = room_id, from, to
  end

  def call
    booking = ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
      room = Room.lock.find(@room_id)
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback, "unavailable" unless room.free?(@from, @to)
      room.bookings.create!(from: @from, to: @to)
    end
    { success: true, booking: booking }
  end
end
pitfalls: A class per script invites 'verb-er' names (BookingCreator) that pretend an object model exists - name the process honestly instead of faking a domain object.
Returning early from inside the transaction block without raising commits the partial state; signal failure with an exception or ActiveRecord::Rollback.
Service objects that call each other's internals form a new coupling layer; keep each script talking to models and gateways, not to sibling scripts.
